[1] On the second Saturday of every month, the basement of the Ridgeway Public Library fills with broken things. Table lamps with frayed cords, a bread machine that will not turn, a bicycle whose gears slip on every hill: residents carry them down the stairs and set them on folding tables. Behind the tables sits volunteers with screwdrivers, multimeters, and spools of solder. Nobody pays for anything, and nothing is promised. The event is called a repair café, and versions of it now run in more than two thousand towns worldwide.

[2] The idea began in Amsterdam in 2009, when a journalist named Martine Postma grew tired of watching her neighbors haul working appliances to the curb. Her first event drew a few dozen people. What she had noticed was simple. Most of the objects people threw away were not worn out; they were broken in one small place, and the place was usually cheap. A five-dollar switch. A cracked drive belt. A solder joint that had shaken loose. The repairs were within reach. The knowledge was not.

[3] That gap between the repair and the knowledge is what the volunteers close. [A] A retired electrician at the Ridgeway café spends most of his morning showing owners where a lamps fault usually lies rather than making the repair himself. [B] He hands over the screwdriver as soon as the owner's hands look steady. [C] The point, he says, is that the lamp comes back next year with their owner already knowing what to check. [D]

[4] Critics argue that the environmental effect is modest. One Saturday of repairs keeps perhaps two hundred pounds of material out of a landfill, a figure that evaporates against municipal waste totals measured in hundreds of thousands of tons. The organizers do not dispute the arithmetic. They point instead to a slower result, one that no scale registers: a town in which fewer people assume that a broken object is finished.

[5] By noon the tables clear. The bread machine turns. The bicycle's owner rides it up the ramp and into the parking lot and the volunteer who adjusted the derailleur watches to see whether the gears will hold.
prompt: In paragraph 1, which choice is most grammatically acceptable in place of "sits"?
explanation: Paragraph 1 is written in the present tense, and the subject of the inverted sentence is the plural noun "volunteers," so the verb must be "sit." "has sat" agrees with a singular subject, and "sat" pulls the sentence out of the present tense that "fills," "carry," and "pays" establish for the paragraph.
subskill: subject-verb agreement in an inverted sentence
